title: GDP, Growth and the Output Gap
summary: What the headline growth number actually measures, and the gap that tells you what the central bank will do about it.

lesson.body:
A country produces goods and services for a year. Add up the market value of everything produced, count each thing once, and you have [[gdp|gross domestic product]].

Three routes to the same total, and they must agree because they are the same transactions counted from different sides:

**Production.** The value added at each stage — a bakery's flour purchases subtracted from its bread sales, so the wheat is not counted three times.

**Expenditure.** Consumption + investment + government spending + exports − imports. The version quoted in the news.

**Income.** Wages + profits + rents + taxes less subsidies. Every dollar of output is someone's income.

The number that matters is **[[real-gdp|real GDP]]**: output with the effect of price changes stripped out. [[nominal-gdp|Nominal GDP]] rising 5% when prices rose 3% is not 5% more stuff — it is roughly 2% more stuff at higher prices.

**Growth comes from two places and only two: more inputs, or more output per input.**

More inputs means more workers and more capital — a bigger workforce, a longer working week, more factories. This kind of growth has a ceiling, because a population and a capital stock can only grow so fast.

More output per input is **productivity**, and it has no ceiling. It is the entire reason living standards rise over decades rather than staying flat.

This is why demographics matter so much to long-run return assumptions: a shrinking working-age population subtracts from growth every year, and productivity has to make up the difference before anything is left over. It is also why a country can run a boom for years without productivity improving at all — and why that boom ends.

Here is the concept that turns GDP from a statistic into a forecast.

**[[potential-output|Potential output]] is what an economy can produce with its labour and capital fully but sustainably employed.** Not the maximum — the sustainable level, the one that does not generate accelerating inflation.

The **[[output-gap|output gap]]** is the difference between actual and potential output, as a percentage of potential:

- **Negative gap** — the economy is running below capacity. Spare workers, idle factories, weak pricing power. Disinflationary.
- **Positive gap** — the economy is running hot. Labour shortages, bidding for scarce inputs, pricing power. Inflationary.

**The gap, not the growth rate, is what a [[central-bank|central bank]] responds to.** An economy growing 4% while deep below capacity gets encouragement; an economy growing 1% while already above capacity gets tightened. Two very different policy paths from two growth numbers that look the wrong way round.

And the awkward part: **potential output is not observable.** It is estimated, revised, and disputed. Every claim about the output gap is a claim about an estimate.

lesson.plainReading: Take actual output, subtract what the economy could sustainably produce, and express the difference as a percentage of that sustainable level.

variables.meaning: estimated sustainable output — a model output, not a measurement

lesson.body: An economy produces $20.4tn of real output. Potential output is estimated at $21.0tn. Nominal GDP grew 5.4% and the [[gdp-deflator|GDP deflator]] rose 3.1%.
walkthrough: Output gap = ($20.4tn - $21.0tn) / $21.0tn = **-2.86%**. The economy is running nearly 3% below capacity.
Real growth ≈ nominal growth - inflation = 5.4% - 3.1% = **2.3%**. (Exactly: 1.054/1.031 - 1 = 2.23%. The subtraction is fine at these levels and drifts at high inflation.)
So: growing at 2.3%, and still 2.9% below capacity.

**Read that carefully — those two facts point in opposite policy directions and both are true.** Growth is respectable. The level is depressed. A central bank facing this keeps policy loose despite decent growth, because the gap says there is no inflationary pressure coming from capacity.

Now the sanity check worth reusing: **a negative output gap plus positive growth means the gap is closing, and the closing speed is what matters.** At 2.3% growth against, say, 1.8% potential growth, the gap narrows by about 0.5pp a year — roughly six years to close. That is the number a rates view is actually built on.
If instead growth were 4.5%, the gap would close in under two years, and the policy path would look completely different on identical current data.

lesson.caption: What the output gap implies
rows: Loose policy, low short rates, weak pricing power in company results.
Policy turns from support to restraint — the point in the cycle markets misjudge most.
Tightening, margin pressure for firms without pricing power.
Aggressive tightening, and historically the setup for a [[recession]].

lesson.body:
**Treating potential output as known.** It is estimated from trends that are themselves revised. Estimates of potential were cut sharply after 2008 — which retrospectively turned an apparently huge negative gap into a much smaller one, and rewrote the policy debate of the previous five years.

**Confusing the level with the rate.** "Growth is back to 2%" says nothing about whether output has recovered the ground it lost. An economy can grow at trend for years while permanently poorer than its pre-crisis path.

**Reading one quarter as a signal.** Quarterly GDP is [[annualised-rate|annualised]], heavily [[seasonal-adjustment|seasonally adjusted]] and revised repeatedly. A single quarter is mostly noise.

**Forgetting GDP is a flow, not wealth.** It measures production over a period. A country can have high GDP and a wrecked balance sheet.

**Assuming GDP growth means earnings growth.** The relationship is loose and mediated by margins, the mix of listed versus unlisted firms, and where the revenue is actually earned. Plenty of high-growth economies have delivered poor equity returns.

**GDP counts activity, not benefit, and the distinction bites in specific ways.**

A hurricane that destroys $10bn of housing and generates $10bn of rebuilding *adds* to GDP. Unpaid care work adds nothing. Environmental damage does not subtract. A country can raise GDP by depleting a resource it will not have next decade.

None of this makes GDP useless — it is the best single measure of economic activity we have, and activity is what drives revenues, employment and tax receipts. But when someone argues that a policy is good because it raises GDP, the honest question is *whose income rose, and was anything consumed to produce it?*

**When a manager says the economy is strong, ask whether they mean the rate or the level.** These imply different things for pricing power and for policy, and the two are often conflated in the same paragraph.

**Ask what output gap their view assumes.** A macro manager positioned for cuts is making a claim about the gap. If they cannot state it, the position is a rates punt rather than a macro view.

**Ask which data vintage a backtest used.** A model fed final revised GDP has information nobody had at the time. Real-time data changes the result, sometimes completely.

**For a private company, ask which part of GDP its revenue tracks.** "GDP plus 2%" is a claim about the whole economy; the firm sells to one slice of it, and construction, government and consumer discretionary do not move together.

**Treat GDP forecasts as a distribution, not a number.** A manager quoting one figure to one decimal place for next year is signalling false precision.

items: Real GDP is the number that matters: nominal growth of 5% with 3% inflation is about 2% more actual output.
The output gap — actual versus sustainable output — drives policy, not the growth rate. Fast growth deep below capacity gets support; slow growth above capacity gets tightened.
Potential output is estimated and revised, so every output gap claim is a claim about a model, not a measurement.
Growth comes only from more inputs or more output per input. Productivity is the half without a ceiling, and the half that decides long-run returns.

questions.stem: Real GDP is $20.4tn and potential output is estimated at $21.0tn. What is the output gap, in percent? Give the sign.
questions.explanation: The sign is the whole message: negative means spare capacity, and spare capacity means little inflationary pressure regardless of how fast output happens to be growing. Note how small the number is relative to how much argument it generates — a 3% gap on a $21tn economy is $600bn of output that is not happening.

questions.stem: Nominal GDP grew 5.4% and the GDP deflator rose 3.1%. Approximately what was real growth, in percent?
questions.inputHint: The quick subtraction is accepted here.
questions.explanation: The exact calculation is 1.054/1.031 − 1 = 2.23%, so the subtraction is good to about a tenth at these levels. It breaks down when inflation is high: at 40% inflation and 45% nominal growth, subtraction says 5% and the exact answer is 3.6%.

questions.stem: Economy A grows 4% with output 3% below potential. Economy B grows 1% with output 2% above potential. Which is more likely to face tightening?
choices: Economy A, because it is growing faster
Economy B, because it is operating above its sustainable capacity
Neither — growth rates below 5% do not trigger policy responses
Both equally, since the average of growth and gap is similar
rationales: This is the intuitive answer and it is wrong. Growth is the change; capacity pressure comes from the level. Fast growth from a depressed level is exactly what a central bank wants to see.
Correct. Above-capacity operation is where wage and input pressure comes from, and it is inflation pressure that policy responds to — even when growth is unremarkable.
There is no growth threshold that triggers policy. The mandate concerns inflation and employment, not the GDP print.
Averaging a rate and a level is not a meaningful operation — they answer different questions.
questions.explanation: This is the single most useful thing on the page: rate versus level. It also explains why markets are so often surprised mid-cycle — the tightening arrives while growth is still improving, because the gap closed before the growth rate peaked.

questions.stem: A bakery buys $2m of flour and sells $5m of bread. A mill sold that flour, having bought $1m of wheat. How much do these three stages add to GDP?
rationales: This sums the sales at every stage, which counts the wheat three times and the flour twice. Avoiding exactly this is why GDP measures value added.
Correct. Value added: wheat $1m + mill ($2m − $1m) + bakery ($5m − $2m) = $5m, which equals the final sale price. Every intermediate transaction cancels.
This adds the bakery's $5m sale to the mill's $1m of value added but omits the mill's purchase treatment. The final sale already contains all of it.
This is the bakery's own value added only, ignoring the wheat and the milling.
questions.explanation: The general result is worth keeping: the sum of value added always equals final expenditure. It is also why vertically integrating two firms does not change GDP even though it removes a transaction from the economy.

questions.stem: "A natural disaster is bad for the economy, so it reduces GDP." True or false — and why?
justifications: False — destruction of assets is not subtracted from GDP, and the rebuilding is counted as production, so measured GDP can rise even as the country is poorer
False — disasters always raise GDP because reconstruction is expensive
True — the loss of assets is recorded as negative output
False — GDP is unaffected by anything physical, since it only measures money
rationales: Correct. GDP is a flow of production, not a measure of the capital stock. Destroyed housing never appears; the rebuilding does. Wealth fell and measured activity rose.
Over-correction. Lost output from disrupted business can easily outweigh reconstruction, so the net effect on GDP is genuinely uncertain — the point is that the destruction itself is not subtracted.
This is the intuition under test. There is no line in GDP for destroyed assets.
GDP measures the value of real production, not money movement. Buying an existing house adds nothing but building one does.
questions.explanation: The general lesson: whenever a measure moves the wrong way relative to intuition, check whether it is a flow or a stock. GDP is a flow of production; wealth is a stock. Almost every paradox about GDP comes from that one distinction.

questions.stem: A macro manager shows a model that would have predicted the last four turning points using quarterly GDP. What is the first thing to check?
choices: Whether the model used enough historical data
Whether it used the data as first published, or later revised figures nobody had at the time
Whether the model was fitted on nominal or real GDP
rationales: Sample length matters, but a longer sample of unavailable data is still unavailable data.

Correct. GDP is revised for years after first publication. A model fed final figures had information that did not exist at the decision date, which is why real-time vintages exist and why results usually degrade when you use them.
Worth knowing, and adjustment is standard rather than a red flag.
Real is the right choice and any competent manager will have used it — this is a hygiene question, not the decisive one.
questions.explanation: This generalises well beyond GDP: any backtest using a revised series is a backtest using tomorrow's newspaper. The same trap catches earnings restatements, index membership and private market valuations — anything that gets corrected after the fact.

questions.stem: A country's working-age population is shrinking 0.5% a year. Its long-run growth potential therefore depends most on which single variable?
choices: Productivity growth — output per unit of input
rationales: Saving funds capital investment, which helps, but capital deepening runs into diminishing returns. It cannot carry long-run growth on its own.
Correct. With labour input falling, growth has to come from output per input. Productivity is the only term without a ceiling, which is why it dominates every long-horizon growth assumption.
Government spending can support demand in the short run. It does not change the sustainable rate of output, which is a supply-side question.
The exchange rate shifts competitiveness and the mix of activity, not the economy's underlying productive capacity.
questions.explanation: This is where a long-horizon return assumption actually comes from, and it is worth noticing how thin the ground is: productivity growth is difficult to forecast, revised often, and yet a 30-year allocation depends on it. Any capital markets assumption sheet quoting long-run growth to one decimal place is being braver than it looks.
